title: Inside the Analyzer: Tube ID, Carryover, Immunoassay Steps and MALDI-TOF
summary: Learn how automated analyzers identify and sample tubes, how sample and reagent carryover arise and are measured, why heterogeneous immunoassays add incubation and wash steps, and how MALDI-TOF identifies a colony from its protein spectrum.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 6 Hits 9, 10 and 11 and Trap 5 (third lesson for Ch. 6). Checked against Armbruster 2014 (read via a page-fetch tool; the Europe PMC full-text endpoint returned an error and direct download hit a captcha), Broughton 1984, Li & Bao 2025, Darwish 2006, Hou 2019 and Calderaro 2024. Nuances: the reviewer says all fully automated chemistry analyzers sample directly from the collection tube, but automation systems may aliquot primary tubes and set the number of aliquots (register flag rv-ch6-primary-tube-aliquot); the reviewer’s “90% species / 98% genus specificity” for MALDI-TOF was not found in the sources, which describe manufacturer score thresholds and performance that varies by organism group and database (rv-ch6-maldi-specificity-figures). Not taught as fact: disposable tips and probe back-flushing as carryover controls, the claim that immunoassay throughput is much lower than general chemistry, luminometer detection, workcell definitions, master lots and the TLA planning sequence.

objectives: Describe how automated systems identify specimens and when they may aliquot primary tubes.
Calculate sample carryover from a high-low sequence and name the routes of sample and reagent carryover.
Explain why heterogeneous immunoassays need incubation and wash steps that homogeneous assays do not.
Describe how MALDI-TOF identifies a colony, how its scores are read and its main limitations.

scenes.title: Three puzzles on the analytic line
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: one morning in a core laboratory. (1) A patient’s low-normal analyte result looks slightly high, and it ran straight after a specimen far above the measuring range. (2) The immunoassay module’s queue grows while the chemistry module keeps up. (3) Microbiology wants an identification from a colony grown overnight, today. Question token: “Contamination, chemistry, or mass?”

cues.text: Invented scenario: a low result looks a little high, and it ran right after a specimen far above the measuring range.
Meanwhile the immunoassay queue grows, and microbiology wants a colony identified today, not in two days.
What links them? How analyzers sample, rinse, wash and identify.

scenes.title: Identify, sample, rinse
scenes.altText: Two cards. Tube identification: on a laboratory automation system the sample-handling module must identify specimens without error using barcodes or RFID labels, and racks and track must take many primary collection tube sizes and types; the system may also aliquot primary tubes and should determine the number of aliquots and sample volume for each specimen (Armbruster 2014). Carryover: the error induced in one specimen by contamination from the one before it (Broughton 1984). Discrete analyzers use a washing step between sample dispensing to avoid carryover (Armbruster 2014). Possible routes: sample probe, reagent probe, mixing bars and cuvettes (Li & Bao 2025).

cues.text: First the tube must be identified. On an automated line, the sample-handling module reads barcodes or RFID labels, and the track must accept many sizes and types of primary collection tube.
Sampling is not always straight from that tube. The automation system may aliquot the primary tube, and it is expected to decide how many aliquots and how much volume each specimen needs.
Then comes carryover: an error in one specimen caused by contamination from the one before it. Discrete analyzers use a washing step between sample dispensing to prevent it.
Carryover has several routes: the sample probe, the reagent probe, the mixing bars and the cuvettes.

scenes.title: Measuring carryover; why immunoassays wash
scenes.altText: Carryover card (Broughton 1984): run two high specimens (a1, a2) then two low (b1, b2); k = (b1 − b2) / (a2 − b2) × 100%. Most analyzers then showed under 1–2%; but with a = 500 and b = 10, 1% carryover gives an error of nearly 50% in b1. Washing the reagent probe between reagents prevents reagent carryover but slows the analytical rate. Li & Bao 2025 found no specific carryover from probes, mixing bars or cuvettes but a cumulative IgG reagent carryover into urine total protein. Immunoassay card (Darwish 2006): heterogeneous assays need a separation step; in a sandwich assay the analyte binds an immobilised antibody, the support is washed, incubated with labelled second antibody, washed again, then the label is measured. Homogeneous assays measure directly in the reaction mixture with no separation.

cues.text: To measure sample carryover, run two high specimens, then two low ones. Carryover is the first low result minus the second, divided by the second high minus the second low, times one hundred.
A one percent carryover sounds small, but if a specimen at five hundred is followed by one at ten, it can make an error of nearly fifty percent in the low result.
Reagents carry over too. Washing the reagent probe between reagents prevents it, but slows the analytical rate, and residue can even build up over many tests.

Immunoassays add their own steps. A heterogeneous sandwich assay binds the analyte, washes, incubates with a labelled antibody, and washes again before reading. Homogeneous immunoassays skip that separation and read the reaction mixture directly.

scenes.title: MALDI-TOF and the hook answers
scenes.altText: MALDI-TOF card: a single colony is smeared on a target plate with matrix; a laser ionises mainly ribosomal proteins; time of flight sorts ions into a spectrum that is matched against a database. Results come in minutes once a colony is available, versus 24–48 h for biochemical methods (Hou 2019; Calderaro 2024). Bruker Biotyper scores per the manufacturer: ≥2.0 species level, 1.7–2.0 genus level, <1.7 unreliable. Limits: closely related species such as E. coli vs Shigella and S. pneumoniae vs S. mitis/oralis; organisms missing from the database. Hook answers card.

cues.text: MALDI-TOF identifies a colony by mass. A single colony is smeared with matrix, a laser ionises mostly ribosomal proteins, and their time of flight builds a spectrum that is matched to a database.

It gives an answer in minutes once a colony has grown, instead of the twenty-four to forty-eight hours of biochemical methods. On one common system, a score of two or more supports species level, and one point seven to two supports genus level.
It cannot reliably separate Escherichia coli from Shigella, or Streptococcus pneumoniae from Streptococcus mitis and oralis, and it cannot name organisms missing from its database.

Back to the hook. Suspect carryover after the very high specimen and rerun the low one. For the immunoassay queue, recall that heterogeneous assays add incubation and wash steps. And the colony goes to MALDI-TOF.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “1% carryover never matters” (✓ after a very high specimen it can cause a large error in a low one); “Every immunoassay needs a wash step” (✓ homogeneous immunoassays measure without separation); “MALDI-TOF identifies anything, mixed or not” (✓ routinely needs an isolated colony and a database match; E. coli vs Shigella not separated).

cues.text: Trap one: one percent carryover never matters. No: after a specimen far above the range, it can distort a low result badly.
Trap two: every immunoassay needs a wash step. No: heterogeneous assays separate bound from free label; homogeneous assays read without separation.
Trap three: MALDI-TOF identifies anything. No: it routinely works on an isolated colony, it needs a database match, and some close relatives look alike.

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Barcode or RFID ID · carryover (b1 − b2)/(a2 − b2) · wash steps”, “Heterogeneous immunoassay = incubate and wash · MALDI-TOF = colony spectrum vs database”.

explanation.what: Plain language: before a result exists, the analyzer must know which tube it has, take sample without dragging in the previous patient, run the test’s steps, and, in microbiology, name the organism. Scientific terms: barcode or RFID specimen identification, primary collection tube, aliquoting, sample carryover, reagent carryover, cumulative carryover, discrete analyzer wash step, heterogeneous and homogeneous immunoassay, bound/free separation, sandwich immunoassay, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, ribosomal proteins, identification score.
explanation.why: Each step can corrupt or delay results: misidentification gives the wrong patient a result, carryover biases low specimens after high ones, heterogeneous immunoassays add incubation and wash steps, and MALDI-TOF shortens organism identification from days to minutes once a colony has grown.
explanation.measure: Sample carryover k = (b1 − b2) / (a2 − b2) × 100% from two high (a1, a2) then two low (b1, b2) specimens; reagent carryover by test sequences such as R1 R2 S1 S2. MALDI-TOF (Bruker Biotyper, per manufacturer): score ≥2.0 species, 1.7–2.0 genus, <1.7 unreliable.
explanation.differs: Sampling the primary tube vs an aliquot; sample vs reagent vs cumulative carryover; heterogeneous (separation, washes) vs homogeneous (read in the reaction mixture) immunoassay; MALDI-TOF (minutes, needs a colony and database) vs biochemical identification (24–48 h).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate carryover from a high-low run, pick which immunoassay format needs a wash, choose MALDI-TOF for rapid colony identification, or name a pair MALDI-TOF cannot separate (Escherichia coli and Shigella).

questions.stem: A carryover check runs two high specimens (a1 = 500, a2 = 500) followed by two low specimens (b1 = 15, b2 = 10). What is the sample carryover?

options.rationale: Incorrect. This is b1 / (a2 − b2) = 15 / 490, which forgets to subtract b2 in the numerator.
Incorrect. This is (b1 − b2)/b1, which ignores the high specimen in the denominator.
Incorrect. 50% is the error that 1% carryover can cause in a low result, not the carryover itself.

questions.stem: Which immunoassay format requires separating antibody-bound label from free label, usually by washing, before the signal is read?

options.rationale: Correct. Heterogeneous assays include a separation step; a sandwich assay is washed after each binding step.
Incorrect. Homogeneous assays are read directly in the reaction mixture without separation.
Incorrect. Fluorescence polarisation is a homogeneous format: binding changes the polarisation without separation.
Incorrect. EMIT is a homogeneous enzyme immunoassay run on general chemistry analyzers.

questions.stem: A laboratory adopts MALDI-TOF for colony identification. Which statement is a recognised limitation?

options.text: It cannot reliably distinguish Escherichia coli from Shigella
options.rationale: Correct. Their spectra are too similar; Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus mitis/oralis are another such pair.

options.text: It needs 24–48 hours after the colony is picked
options.rationale: Incorrect. Identification takes minutes once a colony is available; the 24–48 h figure is for biochemical methods.

options.text: It identifies organisms by their DNA sequence
options.rationale: Incorrect. It analyses protein spectra, mostly ribosomal proteins, not DNA.

options.text: A score of 2.0 or above means the result is unreliable
options.rationale: Incorrect. On the Bruker Biotyper, ≥2.0 supports species-level identification; below 1.7 is unreliable.

Carryover definition, formula, 500/10 example, reagent carryover and probe-wash trade-off; specific and cumulative routes.

claims.note: Not found in the sources read; not taught as fact. The hook answer links the immunoassay queue to extra steps without quantifying throughput.

claims.text: Scenario invented; analyzer and spectrometer drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer states that all fully automated chemistry analyzers sample directly from the collection tube. Armbruster 2014 lists aliquoting of primary sample tubes among automation functions and says the LAS should determine the number of aliquots and sample volume, so sampling may be from an aliquot. The lesson teaches that sampling is not always from the primary tube.

The reviewer’s “90% species / 98% genus specificity” for MALDI-TOF was not found in the sources read. Calderaro 2024 and Hou 2019 describe manufacturer score thresholds and identification rates that vary by organism group and database (Hou 2019 tabulates studies from 98.2% species and 99.8% genus for aerobic Gram-negative isolates down to 62.8% species and 87.3% genus for mycobacteria), and these are identification rates rather than specificity. The lesson does not teach a single figure.
